(i) the effect of adjustment for a third variable on the association between two variables can be positive, negative, or zero, (ii) the sign of the effect of adjustment depends on the sign of the causal effects of the third variable on each of the two variables, (iii) the effect of the third variable is not the only determinant of the sign, (iv) the sign of a causal effect is not the only factor that determines the effect of adjustment, and (v) the sign

(a) in the absence of a confounder, adjustment for a third variable will never increase bias; (b) when there are confounders and a third variable is a mediator, adjustment will increase bias if the confounders are on the causal path from the exposure to the outcome, and will decrease bias if the confounding is on the causal path between the mediator and the outcome; and (c) in the case of noncollapsibility, adjustment for a mediator will increase bias when

(1) the direction of change in bias due to adjustment is determined by a single sign (i.e., positive, negative, zero, or undefined) and is the same for any causal model with the same pattern of dependence and independence among the variables, and that (2) the sign of the change in bias due adjustment is determined by the sign of the product of three terms, which we call the collapsibility ratio, that are functions of the causal parameters of the model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the consequences of adjustments and their detection.
identifying the conditions under which adjustment for a third variable can change or preserve the association between two variables of interest.
the following question: When can we adjust away a source of bias, and when will adjustment increase or even create bias?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the adjustment of a variable for a third variable may or may not alter the bias in an association between two variables.

adjustment can be expected to reduce bias only if there is no noncollapsibility, and that adjustment can increase bias if there is noncollapsibility and the direction of the noncollapsibility is such as to increase the magnitude of the bias.
, in general, adjusting for a third factor may or may not alter the degree of bias, and that it is not possible to make a general statement about the direction of any such alteration.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for any situation involving a single causal pathway, the effect of adjustment is to either reduce or increase the degree of bias, or leave it unchanged, depending on the nature of the adjustment and on whether or not the causal effect is mediated by the adjustment variable.

, when the goal is to estimate a causal effect of X on Y, adjustment for Z can reduce bias in that effect if and only if X and Z are not confounded by a common cause that affects the causal effect of X and Y, and that Z does not mediate the causal effect of Y.

, when there is a causal effect, the direction of the bias introduced by adjustment is the same for all the variables that affect the causal effect and the outcome, and the direction of the effect of adjustment on the bias is the same for variables that affect the same other variable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the consequences of adjustment depend not only on the nature of the dependence of one variable upon another, but also on how that dependence is altered by adjusting a third variable.
the effects of adjusting for a third factor on the bias of an association between two other factors depend on the causal structure in which the three factors are embedded.
the effects of adjustment can be understood by analyzing the structure of the causal graph.
